recent_posts.title: Toasty, an async ORM for Rust, is now on crates.io
recent_posts.summary: Toasty, an async ORM for Rust built by the Tokio team, is now available on crates.io. It supports both SQL and NoSQL databases (currently DynamoDB for NoSQL) and uses a derive macro approach for schema definition. Toasty functions as an application-level query engine that decouples application schema from database schema, handling complex query patterns like conditional updates that are awkward to express in raw SQL. The release is early (0.x), with breaking changes expected, but the core foundation is stable enough to start building with. The author also argues that AI tooling will accelerate Rust adoption, and high-level libraries like Toasty are critical to making Rust viable for conventional web applications.

recent_posts.title: Introducing dial9: a flight recorder for Tokio
recent_posts.summary: dial9 is a new runtime telemetry tool for Tokio that captures a full timeline of runtime events — individual polls, parks, wakes, and Linux kernel events — rather than just aggregate metrics. Built to diagnose production-only performance issues, it helped identify kernel scheduling delays of 10ms+ on an AWS service, fd_table lock contention causing 100ms+ polls during startup, and a global mutex in backtrace::trace. With under 5% overhead, it can run continuously in production. Setup requires wrapping the Tokio runtime with TracedRuntime and traces can be viewed in a browser-based viewer or stored to S3.

recent_posts.title: Free TokioConf tickets for contributors and open source maintainers
recent_posts.summary: TokioConf is offering 20 free tickets to contributors who have submitted a PR to any tokio-rs, hyperium, or tower-rs repository before March 10, 2026. Open source maintainers of projects important to the Tokio ecosystem are also eligible. The conference runs April 20-22, 2026 in Portland, OR, featuring talks, a workshop, and social events.

recent_posts.title: TokioConf Update: What to Expect
recent_posts.summary: TokioConf 2026 is about seven weeks away and the organizers are sharing details about what to expect. The conference is aimed at Tokio users shipping production software, not just core contributors. It focuses specifically on network programming with Rust, covering topics like async cancellation semantics, runtime instrumentation, and production debugging. Tokio core contributors including Alice Ryhl and Sean McArthur will be present and running a Monday workshop. Tickets are priced at cost with a Community Access pool that grows with each ticket sold before end of March. Social events include a Portland coffee tour, a private dinner, and a food cart pod gathering on Tuesday night.

recent_posts.title: TokioConf Program and Ticket Sales Are Available Now
recent_posts.summary: TokioConf 2026 program is now available with talks selected by a committee of Rust experts. Tickets are on sale with early bird pricing through January, with fewer than 200 remaining. The conference takes place April 21-22 in Portland, with a pre-conference workshop on async Rust and Tokio Runtime led by core maintainers on April 20. Social activities and a group dinner are planned for Monday evening. Organizers encourage early ticket purchase due to limited initial capacity.

recent_posts.title: The TokioConf 2026 Call For Talk Proposals is now open
recent_posts.summary: TokioConf 2026, the inaugural conference for async Rust development, opens its call for speakers. The conference will take place April 20-22 in Portland, OR, gathering 300 developers to share practical experiences with async Rust in production. Organizers seek talks covering production lessons, architecture patterns, performance optimization, debugging, testing, team adoption, and future trends. Submissions are accepted through December 8, 2025, with decisions announced in late January 2026.

recent_posts.title: Announcing TokioConf 2026
recent_posts.summary: TokioConf 2026, the first dedicated conference for Rust async development, will take place April 20-22, 2026 in Portland, OR. The single-track event focuses on practical applications of Tokio and Rust for high-performance production systems, featuring talks on debugging async code, production instrumentation, and introducing Rust in enterprise environments. The call for proposals is opening soon, and organizers are seeking community input on relevant topics.

recent_posts.title: Announcing axum 0.8.0
recent_posts.summary: The release of axum 0.8.0 introduces significant changes to the web framework, including new path parameter syntax, changes to the use of Option<T> as an extractor, and removal of the #[async_trait] macro. The update aims to improve the framework's functionality and ease of use, including compatibility with the latest Rust features. Users may need to adjust their code to accommodate these changes.

recent_posts.title: Announcing Toasty, an async ORM for Rust
recent_posts.summary: Toasty is an asynchronous ORM for Rust, prioritizing ease of use for SQL and NoSQL databases like DynamoDB and Cassandra. It generates Rust code from a schema file, allowing efficient data model management. Toasty aims to balance productivity with performance by minimizing the complexity of traits and lifetimes in its generated code. While still in the early stages and not yet suitable for real-world use, Toasty hopes to bridge the gap in Rust's ecosystem for higher-level web applications.

recent_posts.title: Announcing axum 0.7.0
recent_posts.summary: Axum 0.7.0 is announced, featuring support for hyper 1.0, a new axum::serve function, and the introduction of Axum's own Body type. The update also removes generics from axum::Router.
